CHARGE 5.

STATEMENT OF ACCUSED PERSONS 7.
Statement under Section 313 of Cr.P.C of accused persons were recorded on 09.08.2023.
Both the accused persons have denied all the material allegations levelled against them while stating that they have been falsely implicated in the present matter.
Accused Neeraj Kumar has stated that he is innocent and falsely implicated in the present case by the parents of deceased.
He stated that he never harassed the deceased nor demanded any dowry from her or her family members and he kept his wife gracefully with due care and love.
He has further stated that he was present at his home when his wife committed suicide but he did not have any dispute with her on the day of incident or even before that.
He has further stated that there was some dispute between his wife and her family members, therefore, she used to remain depressed and she was a short tampered.

He also stated that due to problem of depression, she used to take some medicines and one day, he received a phone call from police as to his wife was lying on the road in intoxicated condition and she was admitted in Lady Harding Hospital.
He further stated that he does not know as to why his wife was having dispute with her family members.
Accused Sahib Kaur has stated that she is innocent and falsely implicated in the present case by the parents of deceased.

According to the contentions of learned Additional Public Prosecutor for the State, the case of prosecution is crystal clear.
Firstly, it is not in dispute that the death of the deceased was an unnatural death since it was caused by hanging and the same had happened within the seven years of her marriage.

Further, by the combined reading of the testimonies of PW-1 Mr. Ramesh Kumar(father of deceased), PW-2 Smt. Saroj(mother of deceased) and PW-8 Mr. Bharat Kumar(brother of deceased) and other prosecution witnesses recorded before the Court, it has been established that the deceased was harassed and subjected to cruelty as she was objecting to consumption of liquor and GANJA by accused Neeraj, who along with his Bua/co-accused Sahib Kaur also demanded dowry and in that circumstances, the deceased was compelled to end her life.

He argued that the factum regarding torturing of deceased by accused persons has been corroborated by those prosecution witnesses, who are close relatives of deceased, which means that the deceased was harassed to that extent that she was left with no alternative but to end her life.
Besides this, the postmortem report is in consonance to the story of prosecution.

Further the other documents like FIR, seizure memos, memos of arrest and personal search of accused persons etc.
have also been proved by the prosecution witnesses in their respective testimonies.

Thus, the Ld.
Additional Public Prosecutor submits that the prosecution has been able to prove the guilt of the accused persons beyond the shadow of all reasonable doubts and as such the accused persons are liable to be convicted for charged offences.

Per contra, according to Ld. Counsel for accused persons, the prosecution has been miserably failed in its mission of proving its case beyond all shadow of reasonable doubts and therefore, the accused persons are entitled for an order of acquittal in their favour in the present case.
He contends that the allegations levelled in the instant case are vague and not specific.

The postmortem report also not in consonance with the case of prosecution, as there is no antemortem injury found on the body of deceased, which falsify the assertion of the prosecution that deceased was subjected to cruelty or harassment soon before death.
It is highly contended that there was no evidence to show that soon before deceased committed suicide, there was any cruelty or torture committed by either accused.

He further submits that Section 113B of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 has no application because the prosecution has failed to prove that "soon before death', the deceased was subjected to any cruelty or harassed in reference to their alleged demand for dowry.

He also argued that the prosecution could not prove that accused Neeraj had actually instigated or abetted the suicide of deceased as he had no such intention to get his wife died in such a manner and further, the prosecution did not attribute any ill motive on part of accused in alleged abetment of suicide of his wife.

He also pointed out that accused is not re-married till date and deceased was very aggressive in nature and she was also having problem of some sort of depression, as admitted by her mother and brother in their testimony.
He further argued that the accused persons are also entitled to any benefit of reasonable doubt in the case of prosecution.
On these grounds, it is prayed that accused may kindly be acquitted.

V/s State of Maharashtra, MANU/SC/7002/2007 RELEVANT PROVISIONS OF LAW AND CASE LAW :
9.

Before findings, the relevant provisions of law and case law are reproduced as under :-
Section 498A of IPC reads as under :-
Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty- Whoever, being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman, subjects such women to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine.

(a) any willful conduct which is of such a nature is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman ; or (b) harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand Section 304B of IPC reads as under:-
Dowry death- (1) Where the death of a woman is caused by any burns or bodily injury or occurs otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of her marriage and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband for, or in connection with,
any demand for dowry, such death shall be called "demand dowry"
and such husband or relative shall be deemed to have caused her death.
(2) Whoever commits dowry death shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than 7 years but which may extend to imprisonment for life.

Section 306 IPC reads as under :-
Abetment of Suicide: If any person commits suicide, whoever abets the commission of such suicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years and shall also be liable to fine.
Section 34 of IPC reads as under :-

"When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone.
Thus, this provision stresses upon the existence of common intention as well as participation of each accused by committing a 'criminal act', not necessarily in itself amounting to an offence.
Common intention may be proved by conduct, as it can be formed in the course of occurrence itself, and there is no need to specifically prove a pre- mediation or prior conspiracy."

10. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in a judgment Rai Sandeep Alias Deepu Vs. State (NCT of Delhi)
(2012) 8 SCC 21 has observed that :-
"A "sterling witness" should be of a very high quality and calibre whose version should, therefore, be unassailable.

entities.text:
Rai Sandeep Alias Deepu Vs. State (NCT of Delhi)
(2012) 8 SCC 21
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The court considering the version of such witness should be in a position to accept it for its face value without any hesitation. To test the quality of such a witness, the status of the witness would be immaterial and what would be relevant is the truthfulness of the statement made by such a witness.

What would be more relevant would be be the consistency of the statement right from the starting point till the end, namely, at the time when the witness makes the initial statement and ultimately before the court.
It should be natural and consistent with the case of the prosecution qua the accused.
There should not be any prevarication in the version of such a witness.

The witness should be in a position to withstand the cross- examination of any length and howsoever strenuous it may be and under no circumstance should give room for any doubt as to the factum of the occurrence, the persons involved as well as the sequence of it.

Such a version should have co-relation with each and every one of other supporting material such as the recoveries made,
the weapons used, the manner of offence committed, the scientific evidence and the expert opinion.
The said version should consistently match with the version of every other witness.

It can even be stated that it should be akin to the test applied in the case of circumstantial evidence where there should not be any missing link in the chain of circumstances to hold the accused guilty of the offence alleged against him.

Only if the version of such a witness qualifies the above test as well as all other such similar tests to be applied, can it be held that such a witness can be called as a "sterling witness" whose version can be accepted by the court without any corroboration and based on which the guilty can be punished.

To be more precise, the version of the said witness on the core spectrum of the crime should remain intact while all other attendant materials, namely, oral, documentary and material objects should match the said version in material particulars in order to enable the court trying the offence to rely on the core version to sieve the other supporting materials for holding the offender guilty of the charge alleged."
11.

"The Court while appreciating the evidence must not attach undue importance to minor discrepancies.
The discrepancies which do not shake the basic version of the prosecution case may be discarded.
The discrepancies which are due to normal efforts of perception or observation should not be given importance.
The errors due to lapse of memory may be given due allowance.
The Court by calling into aid its vast experience of men and matters in different cases must evaluate the entire material on record by excluding the exaggerated version given by any witness.

When a doubt arises in respect of certain facts alleged by such witness, the proper course is to ignore that fact only unless it goes into the root of the matter so as to demolish the entire prosecution story.
The witnesses nowadays go on adding embellishments to their version perhaps for the fear of their testimony being rejected by the Court.

The Courts, however, should not disbelieve the evidence of such witnesses altogether if they are otherwise trustworthy."

Cruelty has been defined by the explanation added to the Section itself.
The basic ingredients of Section 498A IPC are cruelty and harassment.
13. In Mohd. Hoshan Vs. State of A.P (2002) 7 SCC 414, Hon'ble Apex court held that "mental or physical torture should be 'continuously' practiced by the accused on the wife.

sentences.text: Whether one spouse has been guilty of cruelty to the other is essentially a question of fact.

The impart of complaints,
accusations or taunts on a person amounting to cruelty depends on various factors like the sensitivity of the individual victim concerned, the social background, the environment, education etc.
Further, mental cruelty varies from person to person depending on the intensity of sensitivity and the degree of courage or endurance to withstand such mental cruelty.
In other words, each case has to be decided on its own facts to decide whether the mental cruelty was established or not."

14. Further, in Smt. Raj Rani Vs. State (Delhi Administration) AIR 2000 SC 3559, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that "while considering the case of cruelty in the context to the provisions of Section 498A IPC, the Court must examine that allegations/accusations must be of a very grave nature and should be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

Union of India AIR 2005 SC 3100 Hon'ble Apex court while explaining the distinction of cruelty as provided under Section 306 and 498A observed that "under Section 498A cruelty committed by the husband or his relation drive woman to commit suicide etc. while under Section 306 IPC, suicide is abated and intended.

16. Further, in Girdhar Shankar Tawade Vs. State of Maharashtra AIR 2002 SC 2078 Hon'ble Apex court held that "cruelty has to be understood having a specific statutory meaning provided in Section 498A of IPC and there should be a case of continuous state of affairs of torture by one to another."

sentences.text: 17. "Cruelty" for the purpose of Section 498A of IPC is to be established in the context of Section 498A IPC as it may be different from other statutory provisions.

It is to be determined/inferred by State vs Neeraj Kumar on 13 October, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/37791822/
10 considering the conduct of the man, weighing the gravity or seriousness of his acts and to find out as to whether it is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide etc.
It is to be established that the woman has been subjected to cruelty continuously/ persistently or at least in close proximity of time of lodging the complaint.
Petty quarrels cannot be termed as 'cruelty' to attract the provisions of Section 498A of IPC.
Causing mental torture to the extent that it becomes unbearable may be termed as cruelty".

18. It is clear from the above settled law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in catena of decisions that for cruelty to come U/s 498A, mental or physical torture has to be continuously practiced by the accused on his wife.
Allegations must be of a very grave nature and should be proved beyond reasonable doubt.
Cruelty has to be understood having a specific statutory meaning provided under Section 498A IPC and there should be a continuous state of affairs of torture by one to another.
For proving cruelty, it is to be established that the woman has been subjected to cruelty continuously/persistently or at least in close proximity of time of lodging the complaint.

19. A legal fiction has been created in the said provision to the effect that in the event it is established that soon before the death, the deceased was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any of his relative; for or in connection with any demand of dowry, such death shall be called "dowry death", and such husband or relative shall be deemed to have caused her death.

The parliament has also inserted Section 113B of the Indian Evidence Act by Act No.43 of 1986 with effect from 1.5.1986 which reads as under:-
"113 B- Presumption as to dowry death. - When the question is whether a person has committed the dowry death of a woman and it is shown that soon before her death such woman had been subjected by such person to cruelty or harassment for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry, the Court shall presume that such person had caused the dowry death."
Explanation.-
For the purposes of this section, "dowry death", shall have the same meaning as in section 304-B of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860)".

20. From a conjoint reading of Section 304-B of the Indian Penal Code and Section 113-B of the Indian Evidence Act, it will be apparent that a presumption arising thereunder will operate if the prosecution is able to establish the circumstances as set out in Section 304-B of the Indian Penal Code.

sentences.text: 22. The essential ingredient of Section 304B is that soon before her death woman was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or his family members in connection with demand of dowry.
23. The question as to what is the cause of a suicide has no easy answers because suicidal ideation and behaviour in human beings are complex and multifaceted.
Different individuals in the same situation react and behave differently because of the personal meaning they add to each event, thus individual vulnerability to suicide will vary.

Accordingly, this Court is of the view that before holding an accused guilty of an offence under Section 306 IPC, it must scrupulously examine the facts and circumstances of the case and also assess the evidence adduced before it in order to find out whether the alleged cruelty and harassment meted out to the victim had left the victim with no other alternative but to put an end to her life.
It is also to be borne in mind that in cases of alleged abetment of suicide, there must be proof of direct or indirect acts of incitement to the commission of suicide.

Merely on the allegation of harassment without there being any positive action proximate to the time of occurrence on the part of the accused which led or compelled the person to commit suicide, conviction in terms of Section 306 IPC is not sustainable.
24. Abetment involves a mental process of instigating a person in doing something.

Section 107 of IPC provides that a person abets the doing of a thing when :-
(i) he instigates any person to do that thing: or (ii) he engages with one or more persons in any conspiracy for the doing  of that thing; or (iii) he intentionally aids, by acts or illegal omission, the doing of that thing.
25. The word 'instigate' literally means to provoke, incite, urge on or bring about by persuasion to do anything.

It would be beneficial to refer para 7 of judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in M.
Arjunan's case(supra) which reads as under :-
"7.
The essential ingredients of the offence under Section 306 IPC are : (i) the abetment; (ii) the intention of the accused to aid or instigate or abet the deceased to commit suicide.
The act of the accused, however, insulting the deceased by using abusive language will not, by itself, constitute the abetment of suicide.
There should be evidence capable of suggesting that the accused intended by such act to instigate the deceased to commit suicide.
Unless the ingredients of instigation/ abetment to commit suicide are satisfied the accused cannot be convicted under Section 306 IPC."

12 FINDINGS 26.

In the present case, both the accused persons have been charged for committing offence punishable under Section 498A/34 IPC as they both being the husband and aunt/bua of husband of deceased in furtherance of their common intention subjected the deceased to cruelty for / in connection with demand of dowry during 21.07.2015 and 29.10.2016.

Accused Neeraj Kumar has also been charged for the offence punishable under Section 304B of IPC or in the alternative for the offence punishable under Section 306 of IPC as the deceased Smt. Pinki, who was married on 21.07.2015 with accused Neeraj Kumar died on 29.10.2016 by hanging herself, which was an unnatural death and soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty / harassment by the accused Neeraj Kumar.
27. PW-10
Dr. V.K. Ranga, has proved that the cause of death as per postmortem report Ex.PW10/A was asphyxia secondary to constriction of neck structure as a result of hanging.
Even the defence has not disputed the cause of death of the deceased, who died during seven years of her marriage in unnatural circumstances.

Accordingly, the first question for judicial adjudication before this Court would be whether the prosecution has proven the allegation of demand of dowry and cruelty/
harassment with the deceased for the purpose of getting such demand fulfilled against the both accused persons.

28. In the instant case, the parents of deceased i.e. PW-1 and PW-4 admitted that accused persons had not demanded any dowry before or during marriage of deceased with accused Neeraj and deceased has not made any complaint in that respect with Crime Against Women(CAW) Cell after her marriage in respect of any dowry demand raised by either accused.
PW-8/ brother of deceased has also deposed that accused persosn did not raise any demand for dowry.

It is also admitted fact that accused Neeraj got a job of peon on compassionate ground on account of death of his father and accused was working in the same department where the PW- 1/father of deceased was also working as peon.
In this situation, both sides to marriage must be presumed to be knowing the financial capacity of either side.
Further, it is also noticeable that the marriage of deceased was solemnized in a park near the house of parents of deceased.

Further, accused Sahib Kaur happens to be aunt(bua)
of accused Neeraj, who was admittedly living along with his deceased wife in a rented accommodation and accused Sahib Kaur was residing in Jind, Haryana.

It is also noticeable that no text message or any other proof regarding demand of dowry and any cruelty/ harassment in reference to such demand against either accused has been filed by the prosecution as same could have been available in the mobile phone of parents, brother of deceased or that of deceased herself.
The prosecution has not lead any other evidence for proving necessary ingredients of Section 498A of IPC except the abovenoted testimony of parents of deceased.

In these circumstances, the Court does not find much legal justification for convicting accused persons for charge under Section 498A/34 of IPC.
29.
As regards Section 304B of IPC, it will apply whenever the occurrence of death is preceded by cruelty or harassment by the husband or in laws for dowry and death occurs in unnatural circumstances.

The legislative intention behind the Section was to fasten the culpability of death of a married woman in abnormal circumstances on the husband or in- laws though they might have not State vs Neeraj Kumar on 13 October, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/37791822/
13 have caused her death directly.
Thus, a fiction has been created in the law.
It is because in these circumstances, the misery and agony created thereby which compel the unfortunate married woman to end her life.

An unnatural death either homicidal or suicidal attracts the punishment u/s 304B of IPC and in this regard, reliance may be placed upon the judgment reported in AIR 1991 SC 1226 titled as Shanti vs State of Haryana.
30.

Now coming to the facts of the present case, it is clear from the testimony of parents of deceased,
who are the prime witnesses of prosecution that the deceased was not happy with her husband/accused Neeraj Kumar for consuming liquor and GANJA and she used to object the same with her husband.
It is also clear from the testimony of parents of deceased that accused Neeraj used to beat and abuse their deceased daughter when she used to object to him against consumption of liquor and GANJA.
The said prime prosecution witnesses have not linked the alleged act of accused Neeraj for beating and abusing their deceased daughter for the purpose of getting any dowry.

The Court has already noted and appreciated the relevant testimony of parents of deceased on the issue of dowry and alleged cruelty/ harassment thereto in preceding paras.
31.
So far as Section 306 of IPC is concerned, the prosecution had to prove the intention of the accused Neeraj to aid or instigate or abet his deceased wife to commit suicide.

There has to be a clear mens rea on part of accused to commit the offence under Section 306 of IPC and it would also require and active or direct act which led the deceased to commit suicide seeing no option and such act must have been intended to push the deceased into such a position that she committed suicide (vide M. Mohan V/s State, AIR 2011 SC 1238).

32. In the instant case, the main allegation against accused Neeraj as also reflected from the testimony of parents of deceased is that he used to beat and abuse his deceased wife on objecting him against consumption of liquor and GANJA.
33.

It is noteworthy to mention that in the complaint Ex.PW1/DA dated 06.10.2015, written by PW-1 Ramesh Kumar, the father of deceased to SHO P.S. Tilak Nagar, he mentions that accused Neeraj had beaten her daughter after consuming liquor and his brother-in-law(Behnoi) demanded of a sum of Rs. Five Lakhs and Ramesh Sodhi had threatened him to file a case against him.
Ramesh Sodhi would be responsible if his daughter is killed and their Bua also asks about dowry.

34. It is further noteworthy that the parents of deceased have admittedly not lodged any complaint of any harassment/ cruelty for dowry or instigation or abetment for suicide of their deceased daughter after 06.10.2015 and even thereafter, accused Neeraj and deceased were residing together at their rented accommodation near the house of parents of deceased till her death on 29.10.2016.

The aforesaid complaint against accused Neeraj way back on 06.10.2015 and suicide of the deceased after more than one year therefrom cannot be said to be clinching proof of instigation or abetment to the suicide of deceased against accused Neeraj for want of further corroborative evidence against him.

Admittedly, there is no suicide note written by the deceased alleging anyone responsible for her death nor has the prosecution filed any text message, video etc. thereby proving that accused Neeraj abetted or instigated the deceased to commit suicide with such mens rea.

So far as the alleged quarrel or beating of deceased by accused Neeraj over the issue of consumption of liquor and GANJA is concerned, it may not always amounts to abetment as suicide by the deceased could not be said to be direct result of such beating particularly when such instance of objection to the such habit of accused and his alleged beating to her have been in the knowledge of deceased from the very beginning of her marriage.

Here, reference may be made to the decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in a case titled Sanju @Sanjay V/s State of Madhya Pradesh, (2002)
5 SCC 371.

Accused persons are also entitled to benefit of any reasonable doubt in the case of the prosecution.
Resultantly, the accused persons Neeraj Kumar and Sahib Kaur stand acquitted for the offences charged with.
Their bail bonds stand cancelled and sureties are discharged.

Both the accused persons are on bail in this case.
